turn_text: Are there any other obstacles beyond the pay fors in your mind?
I don't think so. There's a need without question. So I think that would be probably the heaviest lift.

The big number that came out of the meeting was two trillion dollars. The conversation about that is now hot and heavy, like what does that mean, where does it come from, all of that. When you're spending that kind of money, you want to make sure it's being spent properly and you've introduced the paid act which goes to that. Can you tell us why you decided to sponsor that bill and what it means for you?

Well, as I just alluded to, I was a public works and transportation chair for St. Louis County, Minnesota. I understood that to make wise investments using the taxpayers money, it's critical that we do it right. And that's why I put forth a pay to act, you know, preserving America's infrastructure dollars. And really what that says is any federal dollars over 30 million to local projects that you look at the life cycle cost analysis of it, it still keeps the decision locally. Those local engineers are going to make the decision, but this says, hey, take a look at the cost benefit and you make the decision. All it is, it's another opportunity for the taxpayers to understand that their taxes are being used wisely and for great projects.
Have you heard anything pro or con about the bill since you introduced it?

There's some talk about the pros and cons. Some of the other industries have some concern about it. But my goal is not to have the federal government make the decision on what we use on our roads and bridges as far as surface. It allows the local engineers, I'm all about bringing it as local as I can. And that's what I'm most proud of, that the federal government does not decide. what goes on our roads. It's the local engineers and those local project managers.
That's exactly right. That's a great way to put it. I think I'm going to use that.
It's an analysis, not a mandate. Thank you. That's a good one.

Do you think that in the end language like that gets folded into something else, or does this bill, as it works its way through the process, end up being something that goes on its own? What do you think there?

So I'm looking forward to those discussions, but the bottom line is when we invest in our infrastructure, We have an obligation to make sure that we're using the taxpayers' money wisely, and this is exactly what the paid act does.
